lawyer:
Mozammel Hossain with AKM Abdul Hakim, Advocates ----- For the Appellants.
Saifuddin Mahmud with Mahmudul Haque, Advocates ----- For the Respondent No.1
parties:
M/s. Rising Sun Traders Ltd ----- Appellants 
Vs. 
Chittagong Port Authority and anr ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
5. Being aggrieved by this Judgment and order dated 26.9.1988 the Contractor preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 1 of 1989 in this Court and this Court by its Judgment and order dated 15.2.1989 set aside the Judgment and order of the Trial Court and sent the case back on remand for fresh disposal of the suit in the light of the observations made by the Court. The learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong by its judgment and order dated 30.4.1989 again dismissed the suit and rejected the prayer for making the Award the Rule of the Court on the finding, inter alia, that ,the Award was barred by time as the period of limitation of 28 days as per agreement for making reference to arbitration began to run from 24.2.1983 when by their letter the Port Authority refused the claim of the contractor and that the Arbitrator misconducted himself in giving the Award. 

 6. The Appellant-Contractor being aggrieved by this Judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge preferred the present appeal being First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 24 of 1989. 

 7. Mr. Md. Mozammel Hossain, the learned advocate appearing for the appellant contractor, submits that the Judgment and decision of the Court below is illegal and unjustified as the learned Subordinate Judge did not comply with the observation made and direction given by this Court in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 1 of 1989 remanding the suit to the Trial Court for fresh decision and disposal on all points in the light of the observations made therein. 

 9. The learned advocate goes on to submit that the fact that the Arbitrator gave award within a period of 25 days does not ipso facto make the award in valid nor the Arbitrator guilty of misconduct inasmuch as the maximum time limit prescribed for decision to be given by the Arbitrator is 4 (four) months as mentioned in Item No. 3 of the 1st Schedule of the Arbitration Act but there is no minimum time limit prescribed anywhere. The learned Advocate further submits that the Court below committed a gross error in law in not finding that there was no reference of the dispute to the Engineer-in-Charge earlier than on 6.3.1985 when the Chief Engineer was requested by the appellant-contractor for settlement of the dispute as per clause 2.105 of the Contract Agreement before going for arbitration. The learned advocate for the appellant goes on to submit that it is erroneous on the part of the Trial Court to hold that the starting point of limitation would be 24.2.1983. As such the finding, in the opinion of the learned advocate for the appellant, is not based on evidence or on materials on record. 

 10. Mr. Saifuddin Mahmud, the learned advocate appearing for the Chittagong Port Authority, respondent No. 1 in this case, on the other hand, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge rightly found the point of limitation against the contractor and that the Arbitrator misconducted himself by not giving the notice intimating the Chittagong Port Authority that the matter would be decided ex parte and by concluding the proceedings within a period of very short time of 25 days. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has referred to and relied upon the decisions reported in AIR 1955 (Cal) 354, AIR 1956 (Punj) 187, AIR 1974 (Cal) 345. These decisions lay down the principle that the Arbitrator should give notice to other parties about ex parte hearing and also about the passing of ex parte award. But in the instant case no such notice was given by the Arbitrator albeit in a quite different set of circumstances. The facts and circumstances of the present case before us are clearly to be distinguished from those which were before their Lordships in those decisions. In all those cases the aggrieved party appeared before the Arbitrator and thereafter defaulted in making subsequent appearance or prayed for adjournments which were refused by the Arbitrator, and in that context, their Lordships decided that the Arbitrator should have either allowed time or given the parties notice of proceeding ex parte. But in the instant case before us the Port Authority did not appear before the Arbitrator at all nor did they express their intention to appear on receiving notice from the Arbitrator. 

 13. Thereafter, the Arbitrator by Order No. 2 dated 22.11.1986 directed both the parties to submit their supporting documents. The Contractor submitted the copies of the documents in support of their case on 30.11.1986. But the Chittagong Port Authority did not file any document nor did they appear in the arbitration proceedings. 

 16. On that date (14.12.1986) the Port Authority sent a letter (Ext. 7) challenging the arbitration proceeding and stating that the Arbitration case was time barred but they did not care to appear before the Arbitrator in the proceeding. The Arbitrator thereafter kept the letter with the record and proceeded to give award ex parte. 

 19. From the facts and circumstances of the present case, it is manifestly clear from the letter Ext. 7 dated 14.12.1986 and the conduct of the Chittagong Port Authority during the period from the date of the 1st. Order on 19.11.1986 till the date when the Award was given on 14.12.1986 that the Chittagong Port Authority was unwilling to submit to the jurisdiction of the Arbitrator even after receipt of several notices of hearing of the proceeding. 

 21. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances of the case before us when the Chittagong Port Authority received the intimation that the Arbitrator was going to arbitrate on the dispute referred to him they could immediately object to his appointment or resort to the provisions of section 11 of the Arbitration Act for the removal of the Arbitrator. Instead of resorting to such procedure which was available to them in law they thought it best to remain silent even on receiving several notices of arbitration. They remained mysteriously silent althrough, and suddenly on 14.12.1986 woke up and addressed the aforesaid letter Ext. 7 as mentioned above expressing their determination not to participate in the arbitration proceeding and also threatening the Arbitrator to this effect. If you proceed with the alleged arbitration this authority will be compelled to institute appropriate legal proceeding in the court of law." This threatened proceeding was however never resorted to by the Port Authority. 

 22. Another ground on which the learned Subordinate Judge based his finding of misconduct on the part of the Arbitrator is that the Arbitrator concluded the whole proceedings within the period of 25 days. There is no legal requirement that the arbitration proceeding cannot be completed within that period or within a period shorter than that. The conclusion of the arbitration proceedings depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In the present case we find that the other party did not appear before the arbitration proceeding nor did they express their intention to appear before the proceedings. It cannot be said that the decision was given in a short period on time, the decision given within the period of twenty-five days cannot, in any view of the matter, be considered as a hasty decision on which the finding of misconduct of the Arbitrator can be based. 

 23. In proceedings arising out of arbitration, a Court cannot be regarded as a court of appeal from the decision of the Arbitrator. It can set aside an award only on the limited ground set forth in section 30 of the Arbitration Act. If an award is otherwise valid a Court cannot interfere with it or review it.Our superior courts have always expressed opinions in favour of non-interference unless the findings are perverse causing injustice or the Arbitrator has misconducted himself or the proceedings or the award improperly procured or it was otherwise invalid. In the instant case the Port Authority had chosen not to participate in the arbitration proceedings, therefore the contractor's statement remained unchallenged. Still it could not be said in the instant case that it was a case of no evidence. 

 24. Misconduct on the part of the Arbitrator is one of the grounds for which an award may be set aside. But as we have already found that in the instant case the conduct of the Arbitrator in the arbitration proceedings does not amount to misconduct. The finding of the learned Subordinate Judge with regard to the misconduct on the part of the Arbitrator is not based on evidence or materials on record. The law has not prescribed a minimum time limit within which an arbitration proceeding must or must not be concluded although it has provided for maximum time limit of 4 months "or within such extended time as the court may allow" (section 3 read with item 3 of the first schedule of the Arbitration Act, 1940). 

 25. In view of the above we are unable to hold that the Arbitrator misconducted himself or the proceedings by disposing of the arbitration proceeding within 25 days or by not giving specific notice of ex parte hearing or decision and as such the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge on this point cannot be sustained in law. 

 2-105 All disputes and differences of any kind whatsoever arising out of original connection with the contract or the carrying out of the works (whether during the progress or after their completion and whether before or after the determination, abandonment or breach of the contract) shall be referred to and settled by the Engineer-in-Charge/the consultants who shall state his decision in writing. Such decision may be in the form of a final certificate or otherwise. The decision of the Engineer-in-Charge/the consultants with respect to the accepted matters shall be final and without appeal as stated in the proceedings clause, but if either the employer or the contractor be dissatisfied with the decision of the Engineer-in-Charge/the consultants on any matter, question or dispute of any kind (except any of the accepted matters) or as to the with-holding by the Engineer-in-Charge/the consultants of any certificate to which the contractor may claim to be entitled then in any such case either party the employer or the contractor may within twenty-eighty days after receiving notice of such decision give a written notice to the other party requiring that such matters in dispute be arbitrated upon". 

 29. The observation of the learned Subordinate Judge that the contractor remained silent for about 2 years from the 24.2.1983 is not based on fact. First of all, it could not be the starting point of limitation as on that day the Deputy Chief Engineer communicated the decision of the Port Authority while the Arbitration clause required the decision or withholding of decision by the Engineer-in-Charge for the starting point of limitation. Secondly, the documents of the Chittagong Port Authority show that on a complaint from the contractor-appellant the matter was under investigation of the concerned Ministry. The contractor's letter dated 6.5.1986 to the Chief Engineer in his capacity as Engineer-in-Charge Ext. 9(Z) 37 shows that the contractor objects to the imposition of penalty by the Port Authority and requests payment to be made within 26.5.86 and further writes, "In case we do not receive payment" and any letter in this respect from you within the specified time, we will treat it as your denial of payment & earlier by their letter dated 6.3.1985 Ext. 9(Z) 36 addressed to the Chief Engineer, the Contractor referred to arbitration clause in this way, "For settlement of dispute contract clause No. 2-105 or volume I suggests to refer the case to the Chief Engineer (Engineer-in-Charge) before going for arbitration and accordingly we have taken up the case to you 	. 

 33. Regarding the imposition of "penalty" for delay in completing the work the Arbitrator found that it was "not legal and justified" as the delay in performance of the contract work was contributed in no small measure by the Port Authority such as, delay in handing over site of work, supply of materials drawings, adding additional work and for all these, time of performance was extended from time to time expressly or by implication. We find that the Port Authority has no right to impose penalty for delayed performance. The Contract Agreement clause 2.55 at page 41 provides for liquidated damages (not penalty for delayed performance) to be calculated objectively on the basis of formula laid down therein. It is the genuine pre-estimate by the parties of the loss which they contemplated would flow from delayed performance. In the instant case we find that the Port Authority has not calculated the liquid dated damages on the basis of agreed formula, they cannot impose penalty, even their claim of liquidated damages would be very weak as they contributed to great extent to the delayed performance of the Contractor and, further, they condone the delay expressly or by implication. 

 34. In the facts and circumstances of this case we are of the view that the limitation in the instant case will run from 26.5.1986 and as such we are unable to agree with the view taken by the learned Subordinate Judge that the period of limitation will run from 24.2.1983 as by that time there was no reference of the dispute to the Engineer-in-Charge. Therefore, we are of the opinion that the arbitration proceeding was not barred by limitation. 

 36. In this view of the matter, we are of the opinion that the arbitration proceedings was neither barred by limitation nor the Arbitrator misconducted himself not the proceeding in any way, as such the learned Subordinate Judge ought to have made the award the Rule of the Court.
